title: Krell v. Henry
summary: Cancellation of the coronation procession defeated the shared foundation for hiring particular viewing rooms, excusing payment of the remaining charge.

sections.Parties: Krell made his Pall Mall rooms available. Henry hired their daytime use for two days on which the coronation processions were to pass.
sections.Material Facts:
The agreement was recorded in letters that referred to use of the rooms on June 26 and 27, for £75, with £25 already paid and £50 due shortly afterward. The letters did not state the coronation purpose. The agreed factual record nevertheless showed an advertisement offering windows from which to view the procession, and a housekeeper’s explanation that the suite was available for that purpose during the two days but not the nights.

The King became seriously ill and the processions did not occur on the appointed dates. The rooms still existed and could physically be used. Henry declined to pay the remaining £50.
sections.Procedural History: The dispute concerned Krell’s claim to the unpaid balance. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, leaving the result excusing Henry’s further payment in place.
sections.Issue: Could the cancellation excuse payment although use of the rooms was physically possible and the letters contained no express procession condition?
sections.Holding: Yes. The procession’s occurrence on the specified days and route was the foundation of this particular agreement.
sections.Reasoning:
The court examined the circumstances recognized by both parties to determine the substance of the transaction. The windows’ particular location and the daytime-only arrangement supported a shared transaction for viewing the procession, rather than an ordinary lodging contract. The general payment words were therefore qualified by that foundation.

The court distinguished hiring an ordinary cab to travel to a race. Knowledge of the passenger’s purpose would not necessarily make occurrence of the race the cab contract’s foundation; any suitable cab could provide the transport. That distinction makes the special connection between the promised performance and the destroyed purpose central to the reasoning.

Frustration concerns the value or purpose of receiving performance. The rooms’ survival separates this case from the destroyed hall in Taylor, even though the court used the earlier decision’s reasoning about the underlying basis of the bargain.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Krell explains why a contract can be excused even where performing it remains possible: the shared, particular purpose for receiving the performance may have disappeared.

topics.frustration: The procession was the shared foundation for the particular room-hire arrangement.
topics.interpretation: Surrounding circumstances established the transaction’s purpose despite the letters’ silence.
topics.assent: The court relied on a purpose recognized by both parties, rather than a private undisclosed motive.
topics.risk-allocation: The ruling turns on whether the general promise covered the contingency that occurred.
